title: A Warm and Koji Thanksgiving: Slather Your Spatchcock Turkey in Koji Mayo
contentHtml:
An overnight shio koji brine, a garlic-scallion mayonnaise coating, and gentle roasting produce an extraordinarily juicy bird with deeply browned, savory skin.

Another year, another Thanksgiving, and yet another way to roast turkey.

While some details have changed, my basic advice for roasting your turkey has remained largely the same since 2008 or so, when I first started advocating the spatchcock.

Guess what? It’s 2026, and spatchcocking is still the fastest, easiest, juiciest, most foolproof way to cook your Thanksgiving turkey (or for roasting any kind of poultry any time of year, for that matter).

Over the years I’ve made a few adjustments to the process. The most drastic of which was recommending that you slather your spatchcock with herb mayo rather than an herb butter or herb oil. The idea is the egg proteins in the mayo help the bit of herbs and aromatics stick in place on the turkey skin rather than melting and dripping into the base of the pan as butter or oil-based rubs do.

This year’s turkey recipe is, once again, a spatchcock slathered in mayo. However, in the spirit of the Warm and Koji Thanksgiving we’re celebrating this year, we’re adding a koji brine to the mix.

Burn and Learn

This year’s turkey recipe started with a spectacularly inedible chicken. I'd been experimenting quite a bit with shio koji, the Japanese seasoning made from rice koji, salt, and water. It's traditionally used to season vegetables, fish, and meat, and has the ability to enzymatically tenderize meats while also significantly altering the way it browns and the flavors that are produced as it roasts.

I started by slathering a chicken with shio koji (both over and under the skin) and letting it marinate overnight before rinsing the excess off the next day. Then, without really thinking, I started cooking it the way I might normally cook a skillet-roasted chicken: skin-side-down in a hot skillet to get some initial browning before flipping it to finish gently in the oven. But after less than a minute in the skillet, just when a standard chicken might be just starting to brown, my koji-brined chicken had turned pitch black and acrid.

It turns out that one of koji's greatest strengths—its ability to dramatically accelerate browning—can also be a bit of a liability if you're not expecting it.

But before we get to properly using shio koji, let’s talk a bit about koji itself.

What Is Koji, and How Does It Work?

Koji is one of the foundational ingredients of Japanese cuisine. It's responsible for everything from miso paste to soy sauce to sake to mirin. Much of the signature sweet-salty-umami balance of Japanese cooking comes from inoculating rice, barley, soybeans, or other grains and legumes with Aspergillus oryzae, a domesticated mold that grows over their surface, forming a white, fuzzy coating.

[Photo: fo.ol via Flickr]

The mold itself has been cultivated for centuries for food production, but it's not really the mold we're after when we cook with koji.

We're after the enzymes it produces.

As koji grows, it forms a network of microscopic filaments that secrete powerful enzymes, breaking down starches, proteins, and fats into smaller molecules that the mold can absorb and use as nutrients. (For you biology nerds out there, this is known as extracellular digestion. And for you David Cronenberg fans out there, it’s what Brundlefly does to Stathis’ ankle.)

There are three main groups of enzymes worth knowing about:

  • Amylases break starches into simpler sugars. These sugars add sweetness, encourage browning, and provide fuel for further fermentation.

  • Proteases break proteins down into smaller peptides and free amino acids, including glutamate, the compound primarily responsible for the savory sensation we call umami.

  • Lipases break fats down into fatty acids and glycerol, contributing to flavor development.

The really neat thing about koji is that these enzymes keep working even after the mold itself has stopped growing. This is how things like miso and soy sauce develop their deep, savory complexity over months of aging. It's also why shio koji—a simple fermented mixture of rice koji, salt, and water—makes such an effective marinade, even when there's no live koji mold present.

When you coat meat or fish in shio koji, its enzymes begin breaking down proteins, tenderizing the surface while releasing flavor-enhancing amino acids. Those amino acids, along with the sugars already present in shio koji, act as fuel for the Maillard reaction, the series of chemical reactions responsible for the rich aromas and flavors of browned foods.

In raw, untreated meat, proteins needs to first break down through cooking into smaller amino acids before those amino acids can take place in Maillard browning reactions. In meat that’s been treated with koji, however, that breakdown that would typically be triggered by cooking has already taken place enzymatically, which means that the Maillard reaction can take place much more efficiently.

It’s kind of like if you’re trying to turn your Lego spaceship into small Lego town. Before you can start making the houses, you need to break the spaceship into its individual pieces so you have material to work with. Proteases are your kid brother who you let attack the spaceship to break it up into individual pieces, saving you the effort of doing that step yourself.

That's why my first chicken turned black so quickly. I had to recalibrate my expectations of what was possible, and how to get there.

The next chicken I cooked much more gently, skipping the hot skillet altogether. With low enough heat, I found that I could slowly bring the meat up to its ideal internal temperature while developing an extraordinarily deep, dark mahogany color on the skin.

Even better, the meat itself had a juiciness and tenderness that went beyond what I'd expect from a conventional salt brine, along with a wonderful savory complexity and a hint of sweetness.

Which got me thinking: Could I apply the same technique to a Thanksgiving turkey?

Brine with Benefits

Here’s an interesting thing about using koji as a brine: its effects are not uniform throughout the meat.

Salt is made up of tiny sodium and chloride ions that can diffuse deep into a piece of meat. Over the course of a night, as salt works its way through muscles, it alters the structure of proteins, allowing them to stay more relaxed and retain more moisture as they cook. This is why a wet brine or dry brine is so effective at helping chicken, turkey, or pork chops stay juicy as they cook.

The enzymes in koji, on the other hand, are enormous molecules relative to salt. They thus have a much harder time penetrating into meat, which means that their effects—even with an overnight marinade—are most pronounced right on the surface of the meat.

With the deep effect of salt and the surface effects of koji combined, the results are pretty interesting. You can get a tender, savory, deeply browned exterior with meat that retains its satisfying texture and juiciness. The surface of koji-brined meats will also develop a touch of sweetness, deeper complexity from better browning, and some of the savory, pleasantly funky aromas that you get from long-aged meats, even after just an overnight treatment.

And because the surface of koji-brined poultry browns so readily, the good news is that you can achieve those deep, complex flavors without resorting to the kind of intense heat that can risk overcooking the meat.

Flat Out Delicious

For the turkey, I started with my tried-and-true spatchcocked roast turkey technique.

Spatchcocking is the process of removing a bird's backbone (I use some sturdy kitchen shears—you can ask your butcher to do it for you. Make sure you save the back for stock!) and flattening it out. It solves one of the fundamental problems with roasting a whole bird: the breast meat needs to be cooked to a lower temperature than the legs.

With a conventional whole bird, the breast is typically the most exposed part, which is why Thanksgiving turkey is so often cursed with dry breast meat. It can’t help but overcook by the time the legs are done.

Flattening the bird exposes the legs to more heat and helps the dark and white meat cook more evenly. It also puts virtually all the skin on top, where it can brown evenly, rather than half the skin underneath the bird getting soggy.

For this version, I slather my entire spatchcocked bird with shio koji, working plenty of it underneath the skin directly against the breast and thigh meat. Shio koji comes in a few forms. I like to look for brands that contain nothing but koji, salt, and water rather than those with added alcohol or sugar.

I then set the turkey on a wire rack over a rimmed baking sheet and leave it uncovered in the refrigerator overnight, giving the salt time to penetrate, the enzymes to get to work, and the surface time to dry out a bit (this helps with crisping later on)

The next day, I rise off the excess shio koji (including under the skin!), then pat the whole bird as dry as I possibly can with paper towels.

At this point, you can roast the turkey as-is. The koji has already done its work, and even without any additional treatment, you'll end up with a very flavorful bird with beautifully browned skin.

But I wondered if I could improve it even further using another favorite trick of mine: mayonnaise.

I've written about mayo marinades before. The basic idea is that while butter and oil are great for promoting browning, they aren't particularly good at staying put. When you coat a bird with herb butter or herb oil, most of that butter melts and runs down into the bottom of the pan as the bird heats up, taking all those herbs and aromatics along for the ride.

Mayonnaise, on the other hand, is an emulsion of oil, egg yolks, and water. Its thick consistency helps it cling to the meat, keeping seasonings distributed across the surface while the egg proteins also contribute to Maillard browning.

For my turkey, I decided to lean into the Japanese flavors by making a koji mayo, combining three parts mayonnaise with one part shio koji, along with a couple of cloves of garlic, scallions, and plenty of black pepper.

The shio koji adds more of those savory-sweet flavors to the exterior, while the mayonnaise acts as a binder to hold everything in place.

A Cooler Approach to Browning

There's one important difference between this turkey and my conventional spatchcocked turkey recipe: I use a much lower roasting temperature.

Normally, I roast a spatchcocked turkey at a blazing 450°F. It's a great way to get crisp skin and juicy meat quickly. With koji in the equation, however, the turkey would burn long before it cooked through at that oven temperature.

Instead, I roast the turkey at a more gentle 325°F, letting the koji and mayonnaise do their browning magic over time. The resulting skin is deeply burnished and packed with flavor, while the meat underneath stays juicy and tender. I rely on a Combustion Inc. predictive thermometer to tell me when my turkey is done, especially with the confounding factor of how fast koji-brined meats brown which can give a false sense of doneness even when the meat underneath hasn’t finished cooking.

The resulting turkey has plenty of familiar roast-turkey flavor, but with a deeper, more complex savoriness and a subtle sweetness that works particularly well with the garlic and scallions in the mayonnaise.

And since we're already leaning into Japanese flavors, I like to serve it with Japanese Curry Gravy (recipe coming tomorrow!), which takes a traditional rich, dark turkey gravy and spikes it with just a touch of Japanese curry roux. It's not enough to make the gravy taste like a bowl of Japanese curry, but just enough to add a warm, aromatic complexity that complements the koji turkey beautifully.

Every recipe I publish here is personally tested, tasted, and approved.

What I love about this recipe:

  • An overnight shio koji brine adds savory depth, a subtle sweetness, and improved tenderness and juiciness.

  • Spatchcocking helps the dark and white meat cook more evenly and exposes all the skin for maximum browning.

  • A garlic-scallion koji mayonnaise clings to the skin, adding flavor and encouraging a beautiful, dark mahogany crust.

  • Gentle roasting allows the exterior to develop deep browned flavors without overcooking the meat underneath.

Yield: 1 turkey, serving 10 to 12
Active Time: 30 minutes
Total Time: About 18 to 27 hours, including overnight brining and resting

Notes:

  • For this recipe, I recommend looking for shio koji made with just rice koji, water, and salt, without added alcohol. Some commercially available varieties contain alcohol as a preservative. I prefer an active, unpasteurized shio koji for its enzymatic activity. Salt concentration varies by brand, so use a naturally raised, unbrined turkey rather than one that's already been salted or injected with a salt solution.

  • I use regular American-style mayonnaise rather than Kewpie, which I find can develop an unpleasant fishy aroma when heated.

  • Because the koji promotes exceptionally rapid browning, keep an eye on the skin throughout roasting. If it begins getting too dark before the turkey is cooked through, loosely cover the darkest portions with foil.

Ingredients

For the Koji-Brined Turkey:

  • 1 whole turkey, 12 to 14 pounds (5.5 to 6.5 kg), thawed, neck and giblets reserved

  • 1 ¾ cups (420 ml) shio koji

For the Garlic-Scallion Koji Mayo:

  • ¾ cup (180 ml) mayonnaise

  • ¼ cup (60 ml) shio koji

  • 2 medium cloves garlic, trimmed

  • 2 scallions, roughly chopped

  • A few big grinds of freshly ground black pepper

To Serve:

  • Japanese curry gravy

Method

  1. Spatchcock the turkey: Pat the turkey dry with paper towels and place it breast-side-down on a large cutting board. Using a pair of heavy poultry shears, cut along both sides of the backbone to remove it. Reserve the backbone for making stock or gravy. Flip the turkey over, splay the legs out to the sides, and press down firmly on the breastbone until you hear a crack and the turkey lies flat. Tuck the wing tips behind the breasts.

  2. Brine the turkey: Using your fingers, carefully loosen the skin over the breasts and thighs, being careful not to tear it. Rub the 1 ¾ cups shio koji all over the turkey, working a generous amount underneath the skin directly against the meat. Transfer the turkey, skin-side-up, to a wire rack set in a large rimmed baking sheet. Refrigerate, uncovered, for 12 to 24 hours.

  3. Prepare for roasting: The following day, adjust your oven rack to the lower-middle position and preheat the oven to 325°F (165°C). Remove the turkey from the refrigerator. Carefully rinse off the shio koji under a gentle stream of cold water, avoiding splashing, then pat the turkey as dry as possible with paper towels. (Clean and sanitize the sink and surrounding surfaces afterward.)

  4. Make the koji mayo: Combine the mayonnaise, ¼ cup shio koji, garlic, scallions, and black pepper in a container just large enough to fit the head of an immersion blender. Blend until smooth, with no large pieces of garlic or scallion remaining. Alternatively, use a food processor or countertop blender.

  5. Coat the turkey: Rub the koji mayo all over the turkey, paying particular attention to the skin. Place a wire rack in a rimmed baking sheet. Arrange the turkey on the rack, skin-side-up, making sure the bird doesn't extend beyond the edges of the pan.

  6. Roast: Transfer the turkey to the oven and roast until the skin is deeply browned and a thermometer inserted into the deepest part of the breast registers 145°F (64°C), while the thighs register at least 165°F (74°C), preferably closer to 170 to 175°F (77 to 79°C), approximately 2 to 3 hours, depending on the size and shape of the bird and the accuracy of your oven. Rotate the pan occasionally for even browning. Keep an eye on the skin and the drippings, adding a little water to the pan if the drippings begin to burn, and covering any parts of skin that threaten to burn with a foil shield.

  7. Rest: Remove the turkey from the oven and transfer it to a cutting board. Let rest for 20 to 30 minutes before carving.

  8. Serve: Carve the turkey and arrange on a serving platter. Serve immediately with Japanese Curry Gravy on the side.

Note on the drippings:

The shio koji and mayonnaise can produce intensely browned pan drippings. If they haven't scorched, you can strain them, skim off the excess fat, and add them to your gravy for an extra boost of turkey flavor. Taste before adding additional salt, as the koji mayo contributes plenty of seasoning.
